introduction-the-ten-most-wanted.core: The OWASP Top 10 ranks the most common and damaging web application risk categories, based on data from real breaches and scans. It is an awareness baseline and not a complete standard (that is ASVS). Most entries share one root cause: the application trusts input or assumes identity and authorization it never checked. Learning the categories gives teams a shared vocabulary for code review, testing and threat modeling.

first_principles.problem: A team passes a pentest checklist yet ships an IDOR bug, because nobody had framed access control as a vulnerability class.
truths: Attackers reuse the same few techniques.

analogy.title: A police most-wanted poster
analogy.story: You don't memorise every criminal, only the ten who cause most of the damage.
analogy.breaks: The list isn't exhaustive; criminals off the poster still exist.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each PR is reviewed against the riskiest classes.

code.text:
## Security review
- [ ] A01: every endpoint checks object ownership
- [ ] A03: queries parameterised, output encoded
- [ ] A05: no debug flags / default creds
- [ ] A06: deps scanned (SCA green)
- [ ] A10: outbound URLs allow-listed

check.q: Is passing the OWASP Top 10 enough for a secure app?
check.a: No. It's an awareness baseline; ASVS and threat modeling cover far more.

a01-broken-access-control-idor-and-beyon.core: Broken access control means a user can act outside their intended permissions. The classic case is IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): changing /invoices/1001 to /invoices/1002 returns someone else's invoice because the server checked authentication but not ownership. Other forms are missing function-level checks (calling admin APIs), privilege escalation, and path traversal. The fix is to deny by default and enforce authorization on the server for every object and every action.

first_principles.problem: A logged-in user edits the account ID in a URL and downloads other customers' statements.
truths: Checks must be server-side and per object.
derivation: Use **unguessable IDs** as defence in depth.

analogy.title: A hotel key card
analogy.story: The card proves you're a guest, but it should only open your room, not every door on the floor.
analogy.breaks: Hotel doors enforce it physically; in software you must remember to check every endpoint.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Changing the ID returns 404 for other users' objects.

check.q: Why return 404 rather than 403 for another user's object?
check.a: It avoids confirming that the object exists, which limits enumeration.

a02-a05-cryptographic-failures-and-secur.core: Cryptographic failures expose sensitive data through missing or weak crypto: plaintext HTTP, MD5 password hashes, hard-coded keys, or old TLS. Security misconfiguration is the gap between secure defaults and what was deployed: default credentials, verbose errors, open S3 buckets, directory listings and unnecessary features left on. Both are fixed less by clever code than by hardened baselines, automated config scanning, and strong defaults (TLS everywhere, Argon2/bcrypt for passwords, keys in a KMS).

first_principles.problem: A staging bucket left public and a debug page showing stack traces leak customer data and internal hostnames.

analogy.title: A new house with the builder's padlock still on
analogy.story: The house may be well built, but the default lock everyone knows the code to, and windows left open, let anyone in.
analogy.breaks: A house inspection is one-off; cloud configs change daily and need continuous checking.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Stolen hash dumps resist offline cracking.

code.text:
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()               # memory-hard, salted
h = ph.hash("correct horse")
ph.verify(h, "correct horse")       # True; raises on mismatch
# never: hashlib.md5(pw).hexdigest()

check.q: Why is a fast hash like SHA-256 a poor password hash?
check.a: Attackers can try billions of guesses per second; memory-hard slow hashes like Argon2 make that expensive.

a03-injection-the-sql-nightmare.core: Injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into an interpreter's command (SQL, shell, LDAP or NoSQL) so that data becomes code. `' OR 1=1 --` in a login field rewrites the query's logic. The fix is structural: keep code and data separate with parameterised queries and prepared statements, use safe APIs instead of shell strings, validate input against an allow-list, and run with least-privilege database accounts to limit the damage.

first_principles.problem: A search box builds SQL with string formatting, and an attacker dumps the users table with a UNION query.
truths: Interpreters can't tell data from code in a string.

analogy.title: A form where someone writes extra instructions in the name field
analogy.story: A clerk who reads the whole box aloud as commands will follow 'Bob; also give him the vault key'.
analogy.breaks: A human clerk might notice; a parser never does.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Input is always treated as a value, never as SQL.

code.text:
# vulnerable
cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")
# name = "x' OR '1'='1" → returns every row

# safe: the driver sends data separately from SQL
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", (name,))

check.q: Why can't you parameterise an ORDER BY column name?
check.a: Identifiers aren't values; validate them against an allow-list of known columns instead.

a03-cross-site-scripting-xss.core: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection into the browser: attacker-controlled input is rendered as HTML or JavaScript in another user's page, where it runs with that user's session. Reflected XSS bounces off a request, stored XSS is saved (such as a comment) and served to everyone, and DOM XSS happens entirely in client-side JS. Defences are context-aware output encoding (frameworks auto-escape), avoiding innerHTML-style sinks, sanitising rich HTML, HttpOnly cookies, and a strict Content Security Policy.

first_principles.problem: A comment containing `<script>` steals session cookies from every visitor who views the post.
truths: Browsers execute whatever HTML they receive.
Scripts run with the victim's privileges.

analogy.title: A notice board that reads posts aloud as announcements
analogy.story: If anyone can pin a note saying 'everyone hand your wallet to me', and the board announces it with authority, people comply.
analogy.breaks: People might doubt a suspicious notice; browsers trust the origin completely.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Payloads display as text, and inline scripts are blocked.

check.q: Why doesn't HttpOnly fully stop XSS damage?
check.a: The script can still make requests as the user from the page, even without reading the cookie.

a10-server-side-request-forgery-ssrf.core: SSRF tricks a server into making requests on the attacker's behalf, usually through a feature that fetches a user-supplied URL (webhooks, image previews, PDF renderers). Because the server sits inside the network, it can reach internal admin panels and cloud metadata endpoints such as 169.254.169.254, which hand out IAM credentials. Defences are allow-lists of destinations, resolving and validating the IP (blocking private ranges and DNS rebinding), egress firewalls, and IMDSv2 on AWS.

first_principles.problem: An image-preview feature fetches `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/...` and leaks the instance's AWS keys (as in the Capital One breach).
truths: Servers have network access users don't.
URLs can point anywhere, including internal IPs.

analogy.title: Asking the receptionist to fetch a parcel from 'room 1, back office'
analogy.story: An outsider can't enter the back office, but the trusted receptionist can, and will bring back whatever's there.
mapping: 'Only fetch from the post room' rule
analogy.breaks: A receptionist might question an odd request; a server follows the URL blindly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Internal and metadata addresses are refused.

code.text:
import ipaddress, socket
from urllib.parse import urlparse
def safe(url):
    u = urlparse(url)
    if u.scheme not in ("https",): return False
    ip = ipaddress.ip_address(socket.gethostbyname(u.hostname))
    return not (ip.is_private or ip.is_loopback or ip.is_link_local)
# then connect to that resolved IP (pin it) to beat DNS rebinding

check.q: What does IMDSv2 add against SSRF?
check.a: It requires a PUT to get a session token with a hop limit, which simple GET-based SSRF can't do.
